transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-08
Start: 15:00 UTC (08:00 PT)
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Tom Reyes (Redwood SE), Cathy Nguyen (Cedar, Product Lead), Andre Silva (Cedar, Backend), Priya Rao (Cedar, SRE)
Recording: internal/ff/ff-20260708-cedar-002.mp3

Summary: quick triage of intermittent 502s and timeouts observed during the POC. Focus on identifying whether errors are coming from the Redwood runtime vs customer gateway; agreement to run synchronized traces and try jittered exponential backoff + small batch size reduction for next canary. Action items and dates agreed.

[00:00] Maya Chen: ok, thanks everyone for joining on short notice. we want to walk through the 48-hour incident pattern you sent over, go over the retry behavior, and propose a tuned backoff so the pilot can stay green.
[00:18] Cathy Nguyen: thanks, Maya. quick context, since last week we saw a spike of 502s and a bunch of timeouts mostly during our morning ingest window, about 8:20 to 8:50 PT. p95 latency also jumped. we rolled some client retries but that made things a little noisier.
[00:35] Tom Reyes: right, and from the snippets you sent, a lot of the 502s look like gateway responses not returning a downstream body. need to determine if it's from our edge LB or if the Redwood runtime returned 502 upstream.
[00:50] Andre Silva: to be clear, our stack is EKS behind ALB, Node microservices calling Redwood through the hosted endpoint. we have a short 10s LB timeout currently. some of the errors line up with container restarts but not always.
[01:10] Priya Rao: and we did enable our own retry loop with 2 retries, fixed delay 500ms; i think that collided with a couple of bursts and created amplification.
[01:30] Maya Chen: yes, fixed delay with no jitter can cause thundering herd. quick note on Redwood side, we saw increased tail latency for that customer ID during the same window; there were some 502s logged with an internal runtime error code 502X in our traces. but we need your sample headers and request IDs to line up logs.
[01:52] Cathy Nguyen: we can send request IDs; we sanitized them but kept the x-request-id header.
[02:05] Tom Reyes: perfect. for troubleshooting plan I want to try two parallel things: 1) get synchronized traces from Cedar and from Redwood for the 8:20-8:50 windows, 2) run a canary with jittered exponential backoff and reduce client batch size by 20% to test whether smaller batches reduce memory pressure on long sequences.
[02:30] Andre Silva: question, when you say batch size on client, do you mean request batching of multiple prompts or token-batch? in our integration we do request-level batching (we merge 4 short prompts into a single call).
[02:47] Tom Reyes: thanks — yes request-level batching. we suspect at times the KV cache blowup and increased sequence length cause memory spikes that surface as 5xx/502 in the runtime; smaller request batches will reduce peak memory footprint. also jittered backoff prevents synchronized retries.
[03:05] Priya Rao: ok. what about rate limits? we're on the standard pilot throughput, but we did hit a 429 once last week. could that be contributing?
[03:18] Maya Chen: 429s are separate; they don't map to 502s directly but if you have retries on 429 you can escalate overall concurrency which can push downstream into saturation. we can check rate-limit headers in your samples.
[03:34] Cathy Nguyen: timeline: we saw 2 clusters of failures yesterday morning and then a smaller blip yesterday evening. not sure if the evening one was a different root cause.
[03:49] Tom Reyes: okay -- so propose immediate mitigations: - enable jittered exponential backoff (base 200ms, multiplier 2, jitter 0.2-0.5) - cap max concurrent in-flight requests per instance to 8 - reduce request-level batching from 4 to 2 for the canary - Redwood to run a 2-hour tail-latency trace focusing on the Cedar API key and share logs
[04:20] Andre Silva: reducing batching to 2 will increase number of requests and token throughput, are you concerned about cost tradeoffs?
[04:31] Maya Chen: yes, that will increase token count slightly. but for the pilot the goal is stability; Redwood Optimize later can suggest quantization and batching tradeoffs to recover cost.
[04:45] Priya Rao: on the SRE side, i want to know if there's any persistent file descriptors leak or p95 CPU spikes on your service that correlate. do you have per-container CPU/heap traces?
[04:58] Tom Reyes: we do; the runtime sampled metrics show occasional GC pauses at high sequence lengths; but those correlate with the same request IDs Tom referenced earlier. again we need the t+ IDs to correlate.
[05:15] Cathy Nguyen: one more thing — our legal/security asked if this pattern might be due to payload size and PII scanning; some requests have larger text. we want to ensure any shared traces are sanitized.
[05:30] Maya Chen: understood. please remove message contents; headers and request metadata are fine. Redwood will mark logs with party markers and won't store payloads beyond retention for the pilot.

[05:45] --- Technical deep dive ---
[05:50] Tom Reyes: digging into the 502X errors — they appear when a kernel selection path timed out waiting for a dependent op on one GPU while other GPUs were blocked; could be intra-runtime scheduling under burst. on dedicated capacity that's less common but on shared hosted pools you can get queuing pressure at token-generation time.
[06:20] Andre Silva: interesting, so it's not necessarily our ALB throwing 502?
[06:28] Tom Reyes: not necessarily. ALB 502 vs runtime 502 are different signatures; ALB 502 often has ALB request-ids; runtime 502 has our internal trace id and an error string like 502X-INFER-QUEUE. we did see the runtime code for several of your request ids but not all — hence the need for more samples.
[06:50] Priya Rao: if it's queuing, would adjusting concurrency on our side suffice?
[06:58] Tom Reyes: yes partially. reducing client concurrency and batching helps. also we can enable prefix K-V caching for repeated prompts which cuts token work.
[07:12] Maya Chen: also worth trying graceful client-side circuit breaker: after 5 consecutive errors for a user session, fail fast for 2s then resume; that prevents long tail retries hammering the runtime.
[07:30] Cathy Nguyen: for the canary timing, we want to run it during the same ingest window to get realistic load. can we simulate morning traffic?
[07:40] Andre Silva: we have a staging script that replays production-ish traffic; we'll attach it to the action items.
[07:50] Tom Reyes: great — plan for canary: run replayed morning traffic with batching=2, concurrency cap 8, jittered backoff enabled. Redwood will instrument the runtime trace and we will capture GC, GPU queue depth, and internal 502 counters.
[08:10] Priya Rao: question on observability: can you expose token-level latency by request-id in the console for our pilot? we need to map user-visible latency to token generation time.
[08:24] Maya Chen: yes, we can give you a per-request breakdown in the Console for the pilot. we'll generate a dashboard link with filters for your API key and window.
[08:38] Cathy Nguyen: security quick check: we need SOC2 docs and a short network architecture checklist for our procurement team to sign off before we scale.
[08:48] Maya Chen: i'll send SOC2 + SOC2 scoping doc and our support escalation matrix. action item for Maya.

[09:00] --- Mis-transcriptions and side notes ---
[09:03] Andre Silva: i keep hearing K-V cash in the notes, it's K-V cache.
[09:07] Tom Reyes: yeah sorry, speech recog glitch. also you might see 'Redwood dedicate' in auto transcripts — that's Redwood Dedicated, our reserved capacity offering.

[09:20] Maya Chen: quick risk note — if the canary still shows 502s after client-side mitigations, next step is a short dedicated slot reservation for a few hours to eliminate multi-tenant queueing as a variable. that is commit-heavy so we'll only do it if traces point to runtime queueing.
[09:45] Cathy Nguyen: understood. what about retry idempotency? some of our requests are non-idempotent, so retrying is tricky.
[09:54] Tom Reyes: right, for non-idempotent flows add a client-side dedupe token, or better, prefer fail-fast and surface an explicit retry UI to the user. we can also add a conditional retry only for idempotent endpoints.
[10:10] Priya Rao: ok, for next steps on our side we'll: 1) sanitize and send failing request samples and x-request-ids 2) run staging replay with specified parameters 3) provide recent ALB logs for the windows.
[10:28] Maya Chen: Redwood will: 1) run 2-hour tail-latency trace and share sanitized logs 2) prepare a console dashboard link filtered to your API key 3) draft a canary run plan and proposed backoff settings.
[10:45] Andre Silva: timeline acceptable. one ask: can you include an example of jittered backoff code for our Node client?
[10:52] Tom Reyes: yes i'll paste a small snippet in the follow-up email.
[11:00] Cathy Nguyen: thanks, and let's reconvene after the canary. preferred slot next week Tue or Wed morning.
[11:08] Maya Chen: we'll propose Wed 2026-07-13 10:00 PDT.
[11:12] Closing recap: agreed mitigations are jittered backoff, reduce request batching, concurrency cap, send sample ids, Redwood to trace and inspect. deliverables and owners in action items.

Notes about transcript quality: automatic transcription had intermittent name swaps, occasional mis-heard product names, and timestamps approximate. many sentences run together; some technical acronyms mis-transcribed (VPC -> V-P-C, KV cache -> K-V cash).
